title: LR launches new guidance to help shipowners navigate the growing complexity of retrofit projects
summary: Lloyd's Register has released new guidance for shipowners navigating the complex and costly retrofits required to avoid FuelEU Maritime fines and improve abysmal Carbon Intensity Indicator (CII) ratings. While covering alternative fuels like LNG and methanol, alongside "energy-saving devices," this guidance primarily underscores the industry's struggle to move beyond incremental adjustments. Ultimately, this initiative appears more about managing regulatory compliance and asset life extension than driving the urgent, radical decarbonisation needed to curb excessive carbon emissions.
content:
New guidance highlights the practical challenges shipowners face as they retrofit existing vessels for alternative fuels and energy-saving technologies to meet evolving environmental regulations.

Lloyd’s Register (LR) has published new Guidance Notes for Retrofit of Alternative Fuels and Energy Saving Devices highlighting the growing complexity of ship retrofit projects.

As regulatory and commercial pressures increase through measures such as FuelEU Maritime, the Carbon Intensity Indicator (CII) and the IMO’s greenhouse gas reduction ambitions, retrofitting existing vessels is becoming an increasingly important pathway for owners seeking to improve efficiency, reduce emissions and extend asset life.

However, the challenge is no longer simply selecting a single fuel or technology. Retrofit projects have become increasingly complex, requiring careful consideration of fuel storage, engine compatibility, safety systems, crew training, statutory approvals, vessel design and long-term operational impacts.

To help the industry navigate these challenges, LR’s new publication brings together alternative fuels and energy-saving devices within a single retrofit framework. It covers the practical considerations associated with converting vessels to LNG, methanol, ethanol, ammonia, hydrogen and LPG, alongside the installation of wind-assisted propulsion systems (WAPS) and air lubrication systems (ALS).

A central theme is that many retrofit decisions must be made much earlier in the process than owners may expect. Factors such as engine conversion capability, available onboard space, tank location, fuel-system integration and project execution can have a major influence on project costs, timelines and operational outcomes.

The guidance emphasises the importance of early collaboration between owners, shipyards, equipment manufacturers, flag administrations and classification societies to avoid delays and reduce project risk.

The publication also highlights growing opportunities for energy-saving technologies. Wind-assisted propulsion systems, for example, can benefit from incentives under FuelEU Maritime through a reward factor designed to recognise their contribution to lowering greenhouse gas intensity

At the same time, the guidance notes reflect growing industry recognition that retrofit projects must address both technical and human factors. Extensive crew training, revised operating procedures, updated safety management systems and new risk assessments are identified as essential elements of successful deployment, particularly for fuels such as ammonia and hydrogen, which introduce new safety considerations

Paul Herbert, Principal Technology Specialist at Lloyd’s Register, said: “With much of the global fleet expected to remain in service well into the next decade, retrofit projects will play a critical role in shipping’s decarbonisation journey. The challenge is no longer identifying technologies, but understanding how those technologies can be safely, practically and economically integrated into existing ships while meeting increasingly demanding regulatory requirements.

“As the industry evaluates a wider range of fuel and efficiency solutions, retrofit projects are becoming more complex. This guidance has been developed to give the industry a practical framework for navigating those challenges. By bringing alternative fuels and energy-saving technologies together in a single document, we are helping owners take a more informed and structured approach to retrofit decision-making and project delivery.”

The Guidance Notes for Retrofit of Alternative Fuels and Energy Saving Devices is available from LR’s Retrofit Research programme: Ship Retrofitting | Retrofit Research Programme | LR
